question: State one difference between a high street bank and an online-only bank.

points: High street banks have physical branches; online-only banks do not (1)
Online banks typically offer lower fees or higher savings rates due to lower overheads (1)

question: Identify one feature that distinguishes a building society from a high street bank.

points: Building societies are mutual organisations owned by their members (savers and borrowers) (1)
Building societies traditionally specialise in mortgages and savings (1)

question: State two features of a credit union.

points: Non-profit / member-owned cooperative (1)
Membership is based on a common bond (e.g. workplace, community, faith) (1)
Typically offers lower-interest loans and savings accounts to members (1)
Profits are returned to members as dividends or reduced fees (1)

question: State what NS&I stands for.

points: National Savings and Investments (1)

question: Give two features of NS&I (National Savings and Investments).

points: Backed by HM Treasury / UK government (1)
Savings are 100% protected (no limit unlike FSCS £85,000 cap) (1)
Offers Premium Bonds, fixed-rate bonds, and cash ISAs (1)
Funds raised by NS&I help finance UK government borrowing (1)

question: Give two advantages to a consumer of using mobile banking.

points: 24/7 access to account from anywhere (1)
Can make payments, transfers and check balance instantly (1)
Push notifications alert the user to transactions immediately (1)
Eliminates need to travel to a branch (1)

question: Identify two situations when a customer would prefer to use a branch rather than online banking.

points: Depositing a large amount of cash (1)
Dealing with a complex issue or dispute that requires face-to-face discussion (1)
Obtaining financial advice for mortgages or investments (1)
When the customer does not have internet access (1)
Elderly or vulnerable customers who prefer in-person support (1)

question: State two features of a payday loan.

points: Short-term / designed to be repaid on next payday (1)
Very high APR (1)
Typically small amounts borrowed (1)
Quick / easy to obtain, often online (1)

question: Identify two features of peer-to-peer (P2P) lending.

points: Borrowers are matched directly with individual lenders / investors online (1)
Bypasses traditional banks (1)
Lenders earn interest / potentially higher returns than savings accounts (1)
Lenders bear the risk of the borrower defaulting (1)

question: Give two services that insurance companies provide to personal customers.

points: Life insurance / life assurance (1)
Home (buildings and/or contents) insurance (1)
Car / motor insurance (1)
Travel insurance (1)
Health / private medical insurance (1)
Income protection / critical illness insurance (1)

question: State two ways a bank can communicate with its customers.

points: Branch (face-to-face) (1)
Telephone / helpline (1)
Online banking portal (1)
Mobile banking app (1)
Post / letter (1)
Email (1)
Live chat / chatbot (1)

question: Identify two characteristics of a challenger bank.

points: Digital / app-only, no physical branches (1)
Often offers competitive fees or interest rates (1)
Aims to disrupt / compete with traditional high street banks (1)
Uses modern technology / open banking APIs (1)

question: Give two advantages to a bank of offering telephone banking.

points: Reduces footfall in branches, lowering branch operating costs (1)
Allows customers to access services outside branch opening hours (1)
Serves customers who do not live near a branch (1)
Provides an accessible channel for customers without internet (1)

question: State two advantages to a saver of using a building society instead of a bank.

points: As a mutual, profits are passed back to members rather than shareholders, which may mean better interest rates (1)
Traditionally specialise in mortgages and savings so may offer competitive mortgage deals (1)
Savers become members and may have a say in the running of the organisation (1)

question: State two reasons why a bank may still send some communications to customers by post.

points: Regulatory / legal requirement to provide certain notices in writing (1)
Some customers, particularly elderly, do not use online or mobile banking (1)
Paper statements as a backup record of transactions (1)
Security — postal delivery is harder for fraudsters to intercept than email (1)

scenario: First Choice Bank has recently closed 40% of its branches. Customer complaints have risen significantly, particularly from elderly customers.
question: Explain one reason why elderly customers may be disadvantaged by the branch closures.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 for reason and 1 for development.
points: Elderly customers are less likely to use digital channels (1) so they lose their primary method of accessing banking services (1)
Many elderly customers prefer face-to-face interaction (1) and may not feel confident using online or telephone banking, leaving them unable to complete everyday transactions (1)

scenario: Nathaniel works for a large employer that runs a workplace credit union. He wants to borrow £500.
question: Explain one advantage to Nathaniel of borrowing from the credit union rather than a payday lender.

points: The credit union will charge a much lower interest rate than a payday lender (1) meaning Nathaniel will repay significantly less in total (1)
Credit unions are not-for-profit and prioritise member welfare (1) so they are more likely to consider Nathaniel's ability to repay before lending (1)

scenario: Yasmin is looking for financial products and is comparing a high street bank, a building society, and a credit union.
question: Explain two differences between a building society and a credit union.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each difference. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Building societies are open to anyone; credit unions require a common bond (e.g. employer, community) to join (1) so Yasmin may not be eligible for a credit union unless she meets membership criteria (1)

Building societies offer a full range of retail financial products including mortgages; credit unions focus primarily on savings and small personal loans (1) so for a mortgage Yasmin would need to use a bank or building society (1)

scenario: Barclays has launched a new mobile banking app with instant payment notifications, a spending tracker and the ability to temporarily freeze a card.
question: Explain two advantages to consumers of these mobile banking features.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Instant payment notifications alert the customer immediately when money leaves their account (1) helping them identify and report any fraudulent transactions quickly (1)
The spending tracker categorises expenditure automatically (1) helping consumers see where their money is going and make better budgeting decisions (1)
Temporarily freezing a card via the app is quicker than calling the bank (1) reducing the window in which a lost card could be used fraudulently (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award any two advantages with development.

scenario: George has £10,000 to invest and is considering placing it with a P2P lending platform rather than a traditional savings account.
question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to George of using a P2P platform.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for advantage and 1+1 for disadvantage.
points: Advantage: P2P platforms may offer higher interest rates than traditional savings accounts (1) meaning George could earn more return on his £10,000 (1)
Disadvantage: P2P lending is not covered by the FSCS up to £85,000 in the same way as bank deposits (1) so if borrowers default or the platform fails, George could lose some or all of his £10,000 (1)

scenario: Sunrise Bank is redesigning its customer communication strategy. Currently 70% of customer queries arrive by telephone and 20% in branch.
question: Explain two benefits to Sunrise Bank of encouraging customers to switch to online or mobile banking channels.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each benefit. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Reduced number of telephone calls handled by staff (1) lowers staffing costs and shortens waiting times for customers who must call (1)
Online and mobile channels can handle many transactions simultaneously (1) providing a 24/7 service that scales without significant additional cost (1)
Data from digital interactions can be analysed (1) to personalise products and communications for each customer (1)

scenario: Rosa is self-employed with a fluctuating income and wants to open a current account and start saving.
question: Explain why Rosa might choose a building society over an online-only bank for her savings account.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each reason. Maximum 4 marks, up to two reasons.
points: Building societies are mutuals so any profit benefits members in the form of better interest rates (1) which may be more competitive than the fixed rates offered by an online-only bank (1)
Some building societies have local branches (1) which is useful for Rosa if she needs to deposit cash as a self-employed trader (1)
Building societies are covered by the FSCS up to £85,000 (1) giving Rosa the same protection as a high street bank (1)

scenario: A major bank has sent its customers a letter explaining that it is closing their local branch.
question: Explain one reason why the bank sent this information by letter rather than by email.

points: Not all customers will have an email address or internet access (1) so a letter ensures all customers — including those without digital access — receive the notice (1)
Regulators may require written notice of significant changes to services (1) and a letter provides a formal, documentable record of communication (1)

scenario: Patrick has £50,000 in savings and wants full security. He is comparing an NS&I account with a high street bank savings account.
question: Explain two advantages to Patrick of placing his savings with NS&I rather than a high street bank.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: NS&I is backed by HM Treasury (1) meaning the full £50,000 is guaranteed by the government, unlike a bank where only £85,000 per institution is covered by the FSCS (1)
For amounts above £85,000, NS&I provides complete protection (1) whereas Patrick would need to spread deposits across multiple banks to achieve equivalent protection (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: His £50,000 is below the FSCS limit so first mark can credit that he is fully covered either way — accept this nuance.

scenario: TrustBank offers account management via branch, telephone, online portal and mobile app. It is considering discontinuing its telephone service to cut costs.
question: Explain two reasons why discontinuing the telephone service could disadvantage some customers.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each reason. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Customers without internet access or smartphones would lose a key way to manage their account (1) as they may be unable to use online or mobile banking (1)
Telephone is often preferred for resolving complex queries (1) because real-time conversation with an advisor is easier than written messages for complaints or fraud reports (1)
Elderly or less digitally confident customers (1) rely heavily on telephone banking as an intermediary step before branch closure (1)

question: Explain two ways in which payday lenders differ from credit unions in the services they provide.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each difference. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Payday lenders charge very high APR rates; credit unions cap interest rates by law and are not-for-profit (1) meaning borrowing from a credit union is much cheaper for consumers (1)

Payday lenders are profit-driven commercial businesses; credit unions exist to benefit their members (1) so any surplus is reinvested for member benefit rather than distributed to outside shareholders (1)
Payday lenders lend to anyone who passes a credit check; credit unions require a common bond for membership (1) limiting access but providing more community-focused support (1)

scenario: Helen, 72, has always visited her branch to pay bills and check her balance. Her bank has announced it is switching all customers to online banking.
question: Explain two problems Helen may face as a result of this switch.

points: Helen may not own a smartphone or computer (1) making it physically impossible for her to access online banking without purchasing new technology (1)
Even if she has a device, she may lack the digital literacy to use online banking (1) increasing the risk of errors or being vulnerable to phishing scams (1)
Without in-branch support she has no one to help her with complex issues (1) and may feel excluded from the financial system (1)

question: Explain why insurance companies are considered part of the personal finance sector.

points: Insurance companies provide financial products that protect individuals against financial risk (1) such as loss of income, damage to property, or death, which are core personal finance needs (1)

scenario: Monzo is a UK challenger bank with no physical branches. Customers manage their accounts entirely through a smartphone app.
question: Explain two benefits to a young professional of banking with Monzo compared with a traditional high street bank.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each benefit. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Monzo offers real-time spending notifications and categorisation (1) helping the customer to budget more easily without needing to log in to check statements (1)
International spending often has no foreign transaction fees (1) which saves money when the customer travels abroad on holiday or for work (1)
Account opening is quick and done entirely via the app (1) saving the time needed to visit a branch and make an appointment (1)

question: Explain two advantages to a financial institution of using live chat / chatbots to communicate with customers.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Chatbots can handle a large volume of simple queries simultaneously (1) reducing demand on human agents and lowering operating costs (1)
Live chat and chatbots are available 24/7 (1) providing out-of-hours support without needing to staff a call centre overnight (1)
Customers get an immediate response (1) improving the customer experience without the wait times associated with telephone queues (1)

scenario: NorthernMutual is a building society considering converting to a bank (demutualisation). If it converts it will gain access to the stock market for capital but members will lose their mutual status.
question: Discuss the impact on customers if NorthernMutual demutualises and becomes a bank. (6)

indicative_content: Demutualisation means members receive windfall shares / cash payment — short-term gain
Once a bank, profit focus shifts to shareholders not members — potential for higher fees or lower savings rates
Access to more capital could allow greater investment in services and products
Loss of mutual ethos may reduce focus on customer welfare
Banks have more diverse product ranges and potentially more branches or technology investment
Some historical demutualisations led to the institutions later failing (e.g. Bradford & Bingley)
Balanced conclusion required: short-term benefit vs long-term impact on rates and culture

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic description of demutualisation or lists features; little analysis of impact on customers.
Identifies some advantages and disadvantages for customers; some development of points.
Well-developed, balanced discussion of short and long-term customer impacts; specialist vocabulary; justified conclusion.

scenario: BrightBank has announced it will close 200 branches over the next two years, replacing branch services with an enhanced mobile app and a 24/7 telephone line.
question: Discuss the extent to which BrightBank's decision will benefit its customers. (6)

indicative_content: Benefits: lower overheads could allow better rates; app provides 24/7 access; reduced queuing; environmentally beneficial
Drawbacks: disadvantages digitally excluded customers; loss of human contact for complex issues; not everyone has smartphones; reduced support for vulnerable customers
BrightBank benefits: cost savings, modern image
Some customers will genuinely benefit if they primarily use digital channels
Other customers (elderly, those with poor internet) will be significantly disadvantaged
Conclusion: mixed impact — benefits majority of digital users but significantly disadvantages vulnerable groups

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic point about branch closures; minimal weighing up.
Considers benefits and drawbacks for different customer groups; some development.
Thorough, balanced discussion; differentiates between customer segments; considers both bank and customer perspective; justified conclusion.

scenario: Kieran has £20,000 to invest. He is comparing: a high street bank ISA (2.9% AER), NS&I Premium Bonds (~4.4% tax-free), and a P2P lending platform (projected 6% but no FSCS protection).
question: Discuss which option best suits Kieran's needs as a saver. (6)

indicative_content: Bank ISA: 2.9% — lowest return but fully FSCS protected and tax-free
NS&I: ~4.4% tax-free, 100% government guarantee — very safe
P2P: 6% projected but no FSCS protection — if platform fails or borrowers default, could lose money
Risk vs return trade-off central to discussion
Depend on Kieran's risk appetite and whether £20,000 is his only savings
P2P may not be suitable if this is an emergency fund
Balanced conclusion: NS&I appears optimal for risk-averse saver; P2P only suitable if Kieran can afford to lose some capital

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one option; no comparison or application to Kieran.
Compares at least two options; begins to weigh risk vs return; partial conclusion.
Thorough comparison of all three; considers FSCS, risk, return and Kieran's circumstances; justified conclusion.

scenario: FinanceFirst is launching a new current account aimed at 18–25-year-olds. It is deciding whether to make the account primarily app-based or to maintain a branch and telephone option.
question: Discuss whether FinanceFirst should make the new account primarily app-based. (6)

indicative_content: Target market 18–25: highly digital; comfortable with apps; less likely to need branches
App-based: lower cost to operate; real-time features; instant onboarding — attractive to target market
Risk: excludes 18–25 who do not have smartphones or good data coverage
Regulatory requirements may mandate certain communication channels
Retaining some telephone support allows handling of complex issues (fraud, disputes)
Competitors already offer fully digital accounts — need to be competitive
Balanced conclusion: primarily app-based makes sense for this age group but some fallback channel is wise

level_descriptors.descriptor: Generic points about app banking; little context.
Considers pros and cons for the specific age group; some development.
Well-developed, balanced argument; considers target market, cost, regulation and risk; justified conclusion.

scenario: Abena has £5,000 to borrow. She is considering three options: a high street bank personal loan (8.9% APR), a credit union loan (6% APR, requires membership), or a P2P loan (7.5% APR).
question: Discuss which borrowing option best suits Abena. (6)

indicative_content: Credit union: lowest rate but requires membership — Abena must qualify via common bond
Bank loan: accessible to most; 8.9% is competitive but higher than credit union
P2P: 7.5% — between the two; some P2P lenders have fewer protections than banks
Depends on whether she qualifies for credit union membership
Speed of application and approval may differ
If eligible, credit union is cheapest; if not, P2P saves over bank loan
Conclusion must consider eligibility and acknowledge uncertainty about credit union access

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes the rates or one option; no comparison.
Compares options and considers eligibility; some weighing up; partial conclusion.
Well-developed comparison; addresses eligibility, total cost, and risk; justified, contextualised conclusion.

scenario: ValueSave is a medium-sized building society. It is deciding whether to invest in a new mobile banking app or to open three new branches to serve growing areas. Budget: £2 million total. [Table: Mobile app — one-off cost £500k, serving all existing 200,000 customers 24/7; Three new branches — cost £600k each = £1.8m total, each serving ~2,000 new customers, creating 30 jobs; Current customers: 68% under 50, 32% over 50; 45% already use online banking; 20% state they would switch if branches closed]
question: Evaluate whether ValueSave should invest in the mobile app or the new branches. (12)

indicative_content: Mobile app: cheaper (£500k vs £1.8m); serves all 200,000 customers; lower ongoing costs; aligns with 45% already online and 68% under 50
Branches: £1.8m cost; reaches 6,000 new potential customers in growing areas; creates 30 jobs; addresses the 20% who might leave if branches close
The 32% over 50 may be heavy branch users; losing them (20% would switch) = 40,000 customers — significant revenue impact
Remaining £200k from £2m budget after branches could not fund a full app
If app is chosen, £1.5m remains — can invest in telephony or service improvements
Long-term: digital trend favours app; but building society ethos values community presence
Risk: 20% switch risk must be quantified vs cost of 3 branches
Conclusion: balanced argument; likely app is more cost-effective but must address needs of over-50 and branch-dependent customers

level_descriptors.descriptor: Isolated points about app or branches; little application to data; no supported conclusion.
Compares options using some data; identifies financial implications; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation; uses customer data and costs; considers both options; supported conclusion.

Thorough, well-developed evaluation; uses all key data points; considers customer demographics, cost efficiency, risk of customer loss, building society values; specialist vocabulary; clear, justified conclusion with acknowledged trade-offs.

scenario: CityCredit is a small credit union that lends exclusively to public sector workers in a city. It is considering three growth strategies: A) Expanding membership to include private sector workers; B) Launching an online application and account management portal; C) Opening a second physical branch. [Table: Current members 4,000; Average loan size £2,500; Default rate 1.2%; No current online presence; Local private sector workforce 25,000]
question: Evaluate which growth strategy CityCredit should adopt. (12)

indicative_content: Strategy A: opens to 25,000 new potential members — significant growth; maintains non-profit ethos; may increase default risk with less community cohesion
Strategy B: online portal — modern, scalable, low cost; serves existing 4,000 members better; does not grow membership directly but improves efficiency
Strategy C: second branch — high capital cost; limited geographic reach; only serves local area; creates jobs
Credit union ethos: member-focused, community-based; any strategy must align with this
Low default rate (1.2%) suggests strong community ties — expanding common bond could raise this
Online portal best cost-to-benefit for existing members; could also support Strategy A by reducing administration cost of larger membership
Recommend Strategy B with consideration of Strategy A as complementary; Strategy C least scalable
Conclusion must be justified with data references

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one strategy; little or no use of data; generic conclusion.
Compares two or more strategies; uses some data; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation of all three; applies to CityCredit's specific context; supported conclusion.
Thorough analysis using all data; considers risk, ethos, cost, scalability and member benefit; specialist vocabulary; well-justified conclusion with trade-offs acknowledged.

topic: B1 / B2 Financial institutions and communication
scenario: GreenBank is a digital-only challenger bank with 500,000 customers, mostly aged 18–35. A survey shows 22% of customers have experienced fraud on their accounts. GreenBank is considering: A) Investing £3m in enhanced fraud detection AI; B) Launching a dedicated telephone fraud helpline; C) Running a customer education campaign on phishing and scams. [Table: Average fraud loss per customer £380; 22% of 500,000 = 110,000 customers affected; Cost of fraud to bank last year £4.2m; Customer satisfaction score 6.8/10]
question: Evaluate which strategy GreenBank should prioritise to tackle the fraud problem. (12)

indicative_content: AI fraud detection (£3m): tackles root cause; if it reduces 22% fraud rate substantially, saves more than £3m annually; long-term cost-effective
Telephone fraud helpline: reactive — helps customers after fraud occurs; does not prevent it; ongoing staffing cost
Education campaign: cheapest; empowers customers; addresses phishing/social engineering; less effective against sophisticated fraud
Current fraud costs £4.2m/year — AI investment could recover its cost in year 1 if it is effective
Digital-only bank with young customers: less likely to want telephone support; education campaign via app highly accessible
Customer satisfaction 6.8/10: fraud is likely suppressing satisfaction — addressing it could improve retention
Combination approach may be optimal: AI as primary, education as low-cost supplement
Telephone helpline is reactive, not preventive — least efficient use of £3m budget

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one strategy; minimal use of data; basic/no conclusion.
Compares strategies; uses some data; identifies costs and benefits; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation of all three; applies data on fraud cost and customer demographics; supported conclusion.
Thorough analysis; uses all key data; considers prevention vs reaction, ROI, digital customer profile, long-term cost; specialist vocabulary; clear, justified conclusion.
